messages.subject: Re: p value calculation for bootstrapped parameters
messages.subject_clean: p value calculation for bootstrapped parameters
messages.body_plain:
On 01/31/2013 04:51 PM, Felix Sch�nbrodt wrote:
> I have two questions:
> 1. How is the SE and p value calculated in the bootstrap case?

The SE of a parameter is the standard deviation of this parameter value
in all bootstrap samples. The p-value is based on the est/SE ratio
(similar to a z-test), but here using the bootstrap based SE value. It
is not a percentile based p-value.

> 2. Is there any argument *not* to use the percentile p value, which
> would treat the second row as "significant"? What is the difference
> between these two approaches?

There is currently no argument/switch to change the way the p-value is
computed. (But if anyone sends me a patch to allow for more options, I
would be glad to consider it.)

If you need more flexibility, or you wish to compute your own p-values,
you should use the bootstrapLavaan() function. For example:

fit <- cfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939, se="none")
out <- bootstrapLavaan(fit, R=100L, FUN="coef", verbose=TRUE)

The object 'out' now contains all (100) values for the parameter values.
 From here, you can compute any bootstrap based statistic you need.

Yves.

variables. Including the exogenous variables (even if fixed.x=TRUE). Not
only the dependent variables, as you perhaps expect when fitting
regression models only.

This is the typical 'SEM' approach, where modeling the covariance matrix
is the prime objective. Not prediction.

On 01/28/2013 04:36 PM, Alexander Beaujean wrote:
> To the best of my knowledge, lavaan only used the Delta/marginal

> the indicators' error variance to 1 (estimating the underlying
> variable's variance instead), thus making e1-e30 "non-free".

Just to clarify: lavaan uses the 'delta' parameterization indeed (this
is Mplus parlance). It means that the residual variances of the manifest
categorical variables are not free. They are not fixed to 1 either. They
are in fact a function of other parameter values.

Soon, the so-called 'theta' parameterization (again, Mplus parlance)
will be available too. Here, the residual variances are free, while some
other parameters are fixed. I'm considering other parameterizations too.

Yves.

Dear lavaan users,

For those of you interested in accounting for weights, clusters, or strata in your data, a new version of the lavaan.survey package (0.7) has been posted on CRAN today.

A set of example analyses is now available at

     http://wp.daob.org/software/

under lavaan.survey.

Please note that it may be a few days before the change propagates to all CRAN mirrors and the Windows binaries are  compiled.

Best regards,
Daniel

New in this version:
    - WLS, DWLS estimator for complex surveys (similar to the standard estimator for linear regression with complex samples). Requires the development version of lavaan (0.5-12 of 2012-02-07 or later, as usual this is available as install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source") ).
    - WLS estimation with the Yuan-Bentler smoother for the Gamma matrix (gives better results than WLS in some cases)
    - MLMV, MLMVS corrections from lavaan supported
    - New behavior when Gamma is not positive-definite: the estimation is still performed and afterwards a check is done to ensure the standard errors and test statistic are OK
    - Support for multiply imputed datasets (but take care when using weights as well - see documentation)
    - More/better comments in code
    - Example analyses up at: http://wp.daob.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/02/lavaan.survey-examples-paper.zip

messages.subject_clean: saturated correlates in lavaan vs using auxiliary( ) in semTools
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I was trying to compare whether the results will be same if i specify a saturated correlates model in lavaan vs using auxiliary( ) from semTools (actually i was comparing which is faster) and found that the results are different. I am not sure if this should be the case. Here are my codes:

library(lavaan)
library(semTools)

# model for generating data
pop.model <- '
f =~ 1*x1 + 1*x2 + 1*x3 + 1*x4
f ~~ 1*f
x1 ~~ 0.2*x1
x2 ~~ 0.2*x2
x3 ~~ 0.2*x3
x4 ~~ 0.2*x4

# auxiliary variable is correlated with uniqueness
x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 ~~ 0.5*a
a ~~ 1*a
'

# analysis model for using auxiliary function in semTools
model1 <- '
f =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
'

# analysis model for incorporating auxiliary variables using saturated correlates
model2 <- '
f =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4
x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 ~~ a
'

# generate data
set.seed(13243546)

my.df <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs=500)

# 4 missing data patterns with no missing data for auxiliary variables
miss.pat <- list( c(1,1,1,1,1),
                  c(NA,1,1,1,1),
                  c(1,NA,1,1,1),
                  c(1,1,NA,1,1),
                  c(1,1,1,NA,1) )

# create a selection matrix for missing data
selection <- do.call( rbind,
                      sample( miss.pat, size=500, replace=TRUE, prob=c(0.6,
                                                                       0.1,
                                                                       0.1,
                                                                       0.1,
                                                                       0.1) ) )

# generate missing data by multiplying data with selection matrix
my.df <- my.df*selection

# using auxiliary( ) from semTools
fit1 <- cfa(model1, my.df, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, missing='fiml')
fit.aux <- auxiliary(fit1, aux='a', my.df)

# running saturated correlates model directly
fit2 <- cfa(model2, my.df, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE, missing='fiml')

Cheers,
Yonghao

library(psych)

messages.subject_clean: Annoucement: New Versions of simsem (0.5-0) and semTools (0.3-0)
messages.body_plain:
Announcing new versions of both the simsem and semTools packages available on CRAN.  These updates add major functionality to both packages.

simsem provides comprehensive simulation functionality for structural equation modeling. simsem allows data generation based on a user specified model, analyses of generated data, and storage and processing of simulation results. One major update in this version of simsem that may be of particular interest to lavaan users is the ability to specify data generation and analysis models using lavaan syntax.

For further details on simsem see: simsem.org <http://simsem.org>

semTools is a package comprised of useful functions for structural equation modeling in R. semTools is designed to be a user supported package and all users of SEM and R are encouraged to submit functions of ideas for additional functions. The newest version of semTools includes several new functions. One of particular interest is lisrel2lavaan this function will take LISREL syntax files, translate them into lavaan parameter tables and fit models using lavaan.

For more information on semTools see: https://github.com/simsem/semTools/wiki

Thanks,

-Alex

simsem, Version 0.5-0
This version is available on CRAN. Here is a list of major updates:
The generate and model arguments for the sim function can take three formats: simsem template (as previous versions), lavaan script (or lavaan parameter table or a list of arguments for the simulateData, lavaan, cfa, sem, or growth functions), or an OpenMx object. See more details and the example scripts in the vignette.
The generate function can take simsem template, lavaan script, and an OpenMx object. If OpenMx object has definition variables, users need to provide the data of definition variables (in the covData argument) and the model parameters are specified based on the definition variables.
The analyze function can take simsem template and OpenMx object
In the simsem template format, users can add exogenous covariates for data generation, which can take any distributions (or even dummy variables). The KA and GA arguments are added to the model function to account for the effects of exogenous covariates on indicators or factors respectively. Users need to create their own covariate data and add to the covData argument in the generate or sim functions.
Nonnormal data can be created from Vale and Maurelli's (1983) method. Users can simply specify the skewness and kurtosis arguments in the bindDist function.
All arguments that take characters will be case-insensitive.
The combineSim function is added to combine multiple (similar) simulation results into a single simulation result
The sim function has an completeRep argument. If the argument is specified as TRUE, the simulation will be run until the number of convergent replications is equal to or greater than the specified number of replications.
Some minor bugs were fixed.
semTools, Version 0.3-0
This version is available in CRAN. The lisrel2lavaan function is added to translate LISREL syntax to lavaan parameter table with an option to analyze data directly. Many useful functions are added as supplementary functions for OpenMx: standardizeMx to standardize parameters in a RAM model, fitMeasuresMx to find fit measures for an OpenMx output, nullMxto analyze null model, and saturateMx to analyze saturate model. The auxiliary function is fixed to take care all possible models with continuous indicators, is designed to handle the script directly (instead of taking the lavaan output), and is designed to forcefully change the missing option as "fiml". The tukeySEM function is added to Ccalculate Tukey's WSD post-hoc test for multiple group means comparison. The runMI function is fixed to appropriately handle the models with categorical variables and with scaled chi-square values. The runMI function is also fixed to provide the standard errors of standardized solutions for the lavaan 0.5-12 or higher. The fmi function is added to calculate fraction missings of means and variances of data with missing values.

On 02/12/2013 07:04 PM, scott mcloud wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I'm using lavaan to simulate data from a CFA with one latent variable
> with loading factors specified in the population model we're simulating
> the data from.  We then want to fit the data to a general model with
> loading factors unspecified to see if we can recover the loading factor
> values.
> My question is: how can we specify the population model using
> standardized loadings?

The short answer is: install the dev version of lavaan (0.5-12), and use
simulateData() with the standardized=TRUE flag.

Th long answer for the current version of lavaan (0.5-11):

If you want to specify *standardized* population model parameters
(factor loadings, regressions, correlations), you need to make sure that
in your model syntax, the population values are chosen such that:
1) the model-implied variances of the latent variables are 1.0
2) the model-implied variances of the observed variables are 1.0

For exogenous observed/latent variables, you can simply set the variance
to 1.0. But for endogenous observed/latent variables, you need to
carefully choose the correct values for the residual variances (taking
into account the other parameter values). For complicated models, this
may not be so trivial, but for simple models, you can do this easily:
this is an example for a 2-factor CFA:

library(lavaan)

pop.model <- ' f1 =~ 0.6*y1 + 0.5*y2 + 0.4*y3
                f2 =~ 0.6*y4 + 0.5*y5 + 0.4*y6
                # standardized latent (exogenous)
                f1 ~~ 1*f1
                f2 ~~ 1*f2
                f1 ~~ 0.2*f2
                # standardize observed (endogenous)
                y1 ~~ (1 - 0.6^2)*y1
                y2 ~~ (1 - 0.5^2)*y2
                y3 ~~ (1 - 0.4^2)*y3
                y4 ~~ (1 - 0.6^2)*y4
                y5 ~~ (1 - 0.5^2)*y5
                y6 ~~ (1 - 0.4^2)*y6
              '

dat <- simulateData(pop.model, sample.nobs=10000L, empirical=TRUE,
                     return.fit=TRUE)
parTable(attr(dat,"fit"))
fitted(attr(dat,"fit"))

model <- ' f1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3
            f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6 '
fit <- cfa(model, data=dat, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE)
summary(fit, standardized=TRUE)

Sarah,

You can use identical labels to constrain parameters.  The "group.equal" argument is helpful when you want to make the same constraint across (e.g.) all all intercepts for all groups.  I'm not familiar with identification rules for formative indicators (did you mean to use traditional measurement with the "=~" operator?), but your syntax might look like this:

MyModel<-'
Inhibit <- I1 + I2 + I3
Update <- U1 + U2 + U3
Switch <- S1 + S2 + S3

FR<- FR1 + FR2 + FR3 + FR4

## selected mean constraints
Inhibit ~ c(mean1, mean1)*1
Update ~ c(mean2, mean2)*1
Switch ~ c(mean3, mean3)*1
'

fit <- cfa (MyModel, data=data, missing = "ML", group="FRcorrect4", group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))

This is assuming your "FRcorrect4" variable has only 2 levels.  If there are K levels, you would need to repeat the labels in parentheses K times instead of 2 times.  Any labels that are different are unique freely estimated parameters, so you can also allow 1 of 3 groups to be different by (e.g.) "Inhibit ~ c(mean1, mean2, mean2)*1"

Terry

If you must constrain the means to be equal across all groups, you
should fix them to zero. The means of the first group can not be
estimated (without further constraints).

So using this call:

fit <- cfa (MyModel, data=data, missing = "ML", group="FRcorrect4",
group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))

the means in the first group are fixed to zero, the means in the other
groups are estimated.

If you request 'equal means':

fit <- cfa (MyModel, data=data, missing = "ML", group="FRcorrect4",

group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts","means"))

all means will be zero. But if you specify something like

Inhibit ~ c(m1,m1)~1

you will free up the mean in the first group, while it is not identified
(causing the Error in solve.default(E)...)

If you have more than 2 groups, you could constrain the (estimated)
means of the remaining groups to be equal, as long as the first one
remains zero, eg

Inhibit ~ c(0,m1,m1,m1)*1

Hope this helps,

Yves.

On 02/15/2013 03:45 PM, Bill Shipley wrote:
> Hello.  I am relatively new to lavaan.  I am familiar with the use of
> Wald (fixing a free parameter to zero) and Lagrange multiplier tests
> (estimating a parameter than had been fixed) the context of
> modifications of an SEM.  However, I do not understand the output of the
> modindices() command in lavaan.  What tests does this command do?

They are Langrange multiplier tests, for a single parameter only. Often
called score tests. Or modification indices. The latter termed coined in
this paper:

Sorbom, D. (1989) Model modification. Psychometrika 54, 371ï¿½384.

> notice that there is an "epc" column (expected parameter change) but is
> this the change in the model X2 if a particular parameter is freed

No. The 'mi' column contains the 'modification index', or the (expected)
change of the chi-square test statistic. This is the score/LM test
statistic. The 'epc' column is the expected change for the parameter
estimate (if we would make it free). The remaining columns (epc.std,
...) are various standardized versions of this epc value, similar to
parameterEstimates().

The EPC values are based on

On 02/16/2013 12:16 AM, kma...@aol.com wrote:
>
> The version history page states "simulateData() supports thresholds and
> creates ordinal data".  Where can I find an explanation of the syntax
> for specifying thresholds to simulate ordinal data?

Nowhere I'm afraid. Once the 'categorical part' of lavaan has more or
less stabilized, I will write out full documentation.

Importantly, the implementation (for ordinal variables) has changed in
0.5-12 (which will be released next week, but you can install it by
typing in R):

install.packages("lavaan", repos="http://www.da.ugent.be", type="source")

To generate 'ordinal' data, you need to specify the threshold values.
For example:

pop.model <- ' f1 =~ u1 + u2 + u3
                f2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6

                u1 | 0*t1
                u2 | -1.5*t1 + 0.1*t2 + 1.2*t3
                u3 | -0.5*t1 + 0.5*t2
              '

Here, u1, u2 and u3 are ordinal. u1 is binary, hence has only a single
threshold. u2 has 4 categories, and u3 has 3 categories. The thresholds
assume that the latent response variables follow a standardized normal
distribution. If no thresholds are defined, lavaan assumes the variable
is continuous.

When generating data, integers are used for the ordinal/binary
variables, but we do not explicitly set the 'ordered' flag.

 > simulateData(model, sample.nobs=10)

lavaan uses nlminb() per default; the control() argument can be used to

library(lavaan)

eval.max = 20000L

It seems to me that the order of standard deviations are different between two models. In the Stata, you used

ssd set sd 15.23 10.15 16.27 1.01

but in R you used

c(1.01, 15.23, 10.15, 16.27)

The variable names corresponding to rows and columns in the correlation matrix in both analyses are different too. The following script should match Stata and Mplus

vars <- c("EE","DR","RO","SE")
sds <- c(15.23, 10.15, 16.27, 1.01)

lower.cormat <- '
1,
0.25, 1,
0.78, 0.21, 1 ,
-0.47, -0.27, -0.35, 1
'
cormat <- getCov(lower.cormat,names=vars)
covmat <- cor2cov(cormat,sds)
cleary.model <- '
EE ~ SE
DR ~ EE
RO ~ EE
RO ~ DR
'
fit <- sem(cleary.model, sample.cov=covmat, sample.nobs=321)
summary(fit, standardized=TRUE)

lavaan (0.5-11) converged normally after  26 iterations

  Number of observations                           321

  Estimator                                         ML

  Minimum Function Test Statistic               10.781
  Degrees of freedom                                 2
  P-value (Chi-square)                           0.005

messages.subject: Re: Getting p values for variance estimates?
messages.subject_clean: Getting p values for variance estimates?
messages.body_plain:
If you really want the p-value of the variances, you may use the parameterEstimates function to get the p values of all parameters. I would recommend you to not trust the p values of the variances, however, because it hardly follows a normal distribution (except in a "large" sample). You may consider using bootstrap approach by specifying

se = "boot"

in the growth function. Then, use the parameterEstimates function again to get the bootstrap confidence intervals.

Sunthud
